newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, rebels talk, but no breakthrough in crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru, rebels talk, but no breakthrough in crisis.

text.p: Peruvian government negotiators and Marxist rebels held another face-to-face meeting on Monday, but there was little sign of a quick breakthrough in talks to end the 69-day Lima hostage crisis without bloodshed.

A statement issued by guarantors overseeing the talks merely said that Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa and government negotiator Domingo Palermo met in a "cordial atmosphere" and broached "important issues."

The statement, read in Spanish by the Vatican's representative Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani and in English by Canada's ambassador Anthony Vincent, added that a sixth round of negotiations would be held on Tuesday.
Cerpa and his deputy Rolly Rojas were driven back to the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence in a white Red Cross car from a safe house where the two-and-a-half hour meeting was held.

When they left the diplomatic compound earlier in the morning, their fellow rebels cheered, broadcast a revolutionary anthem commemorating dead comrades and bellowed defiant slogans. "We are the ones who have taken the Japanese residence. Until death, damn it!" they shouted.
Also at the meeting was Palermo's adviser, Jose Antonio Payet, Red Cross representative and third guarantor Michel Minnig, and the Japanese government's observer Terusuke Terada.

A metal detector was used to ensure nobody took arms into the two-story building flying Red Cross flags. It was the fifth meeting since talks began on Feb. 11 after weeks of intransigence over the rebels' central demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades.
President Alberto Fujimori said over the weekend that talks were still at a "preliminary" stage although Cerpa's presence was "a small advance" towards a peaceful solution.

In comments published on Monday by local media, Fujimori also said his intelligence services had known the MRTA was planning an assault in Lima and "we could have suspected with a higher percentage of possibility that (the target) might be the Japanese embassy."

A secret intelligence report obtained by Reuters showed that a regional anti-terrorist police unit warned headquarters in Lima weeks before the takeover that the MRTA was planning just such an assault around Nov. 30.

The unit said the MRTA had infiltrated heavily-armed fighters into Lima to form an elite squad to carry out high- profile operations. "Among the actions to be carried out would be the abduction of political and/or military personalities who would be used to pressure the government into releasing Tupac Amaru terrorist criminals in prison," it said.

Rebels initially seized hundreds of guests at the residence on Dec.17 but have released all but 72, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassador's and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
